lessons.title: Asking for directions
lessons.content:
To ask where something is, say ¿Dónde está el baño? (Where is the bathroom?) or ¿Cómo llego a la estación? (How do I get to the station?). Start politely with Perdón or Disculpe.

Useful answers: Gira a la derecha (turn right), Gira a la izquierda (turn left), Sigue todo recto (keep going straight). Está cerca means it is close and Está lejos means it is far.

questions.text: How do you say 'turn left'?
What does 'Está cerca' mean?

lessons.title: Present tense of -ar verbs
lessons.content:
Regular verbs that end in -ar, like hablar (to speak), drop the -ar and take these endings: -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an.

hablar: yo hablo, tú hablas, él/ella habla, nosotros hablamos, vosotros habláis, ellos hablan. The same pattern works for trabajar, estudiar and caminar.

questions.text: Complete: 'Yo ___ español' (hablar).
Complete: 'Nosotros ___' (trabajar).

lessons.title: Ser vs estar
lessons.content:
Spanish has two verbs for 'to be'. Use ser for identity, origin, profession, characteristics and the time or place of an event: Soy estudiante. Ella es de México. La fiesta es en mi casa.

Use estar for location and for temporary states or feelings: Los libros están en la mesa. Estoy cansado (I am tired). Changing the verb can change the meaning: Soy aburrido means 'I am boring', but Estoy aburrido means 'I am bored'.

questions.text: Complete: 'Ella ___ de México.'
Complete: 'Los libros ___ en la mesa.'
Which sentence means 'I am tired'?

lessons.title: The preterite (finished past)
lessons.content:
The preterite describes an action that is finished. For -ar verbs: hablé, hablaste, habló, hablamos, hablaron. For -er and -ir verbs: comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comieron.

Notice the accents on yo and él/ella forms: hablé, habló, comí, comió. They change the meaning, because hablo (present) and habló (past) are different words.

questions.text: Complete: 'Yo ___ pizza ayer' (comer).
Complete: 'Ellos ___ con el profesor' (hablar).
What does 'Ella vivió en Madrid' mean?

lessons.title: The present subjunctive
lessons.content:
The subjunctive is used after expressions of wishes, doubt and emotion, when the subject changes: Quiero que hables más despacio. Espero que estés bien. Dudo que ella venga.

To form it, take the yo form of the present tense, drop the -o, and switch the vowel: hablar becomes hable, comer becomes coma. Some verbs are irregular: estar becomes esté, ir becomes vaya, venir becomes venga. Expressions of certainty such as Sé que or Creo que use the normal indicative.

questions.text: Complete: 'Espero que tú ___ bien.'
Complete: 'Quiero que ella ___ a la fiesta' (venir).
Which phrase usually triggers the subjunctive?

lessons.title: Por vs para
lessons.content:
Para points to a purpose, a destination, a deadline or a recipient: Este regalo es para ti. Estudio para aprender. Salgo para Madrid mañana. Necesito el informe para el lunes.

Por points to a cause, a duration, an exchange or movement through a place: Gracias por tu ayuda. Estudié por dos horas. Pagué diez pesos por el libro. Camino por el parque.

questions.text: Complete: 'Este regalo es ___ ti.'
Complete: 'Gracias ___ tu ayuda.'
Which sentence uses the destination meaning?
options: Pagué diez pesos por el libro

skills.title: Intro to Python
skills.description: Learn to write simple Python programs.

lessons.title: Lists
lessons.content:
A list holds several values in order and can be changed. Write it with square brackets: fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'mango'].

Indexes start at 0, so fruits[0] is 'apple'. Use fruits[-1] for the last item, len(fruits) for the size, and fruits.append('grape') to add an item at the end.

questions.text: What is the index of the first item in a list?
Which method adds an item to the end of a list?

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.content:
A function is a named block of code you can reuse. Define it with def, give it parameters, and use return to send back a result:

def greet(name):
    return 'Hello ' + name

Call it with greet('Ana'). The function runs, returns 'Hello Ana', and ends.

questions.text: Which keyword defines a function?
What does return do?
options: Sends a value back and ends the function

lessons.title: Dictionaries
lessons.content:
A dictionary stores key-value pairs in curly braces: ages = {'Ana': 20, 'Ben': 25}. Read a value with ages['Ana'], or use ages.get('Cy', 0) to get a default instead of an error when the key is missing.

Keys are unique. Assigning to an existing key replaces its value: ages['Ana'] = 21. Loop over pairs with for name, age in ages.items().

questions.text: How do you read the value stored for the key 'Ana'?
What does ages.get('Cy', 0) return if 'Cy' is not a key?
What happens if you assign a value to a key that already exists?

lessons.title: Files and exceptions
lessons.content:
Open a file with a with statement so it closes automatically, even if something fails:

with open('notes.txt', 'r') as f:
    text = f.read()

Modes: 'r' reads, 'w' erases and writes, 'a' appends to the end. To handle errors, put risky code in try and handle the problem in except, for example except FileNotFoundError.

questions.text: Which file mode adds text to the end without erasing the file?
Why use a with statement to open a file?
options: It creates the file if missing

questions.text: Which block runs when an error happens inside try?

lessons.title: List comprehensions and generators
lessons.content:
A list comprehension builds a list in one line: squares = [n * n for n in range(5)] gives [0, 1, 4, 9, 16]. Add a condition at the end to filter: evens = [n for n in range(6) if n % 2 == 0] gives [0, 2, 4].

A generator expression uses round brackets: (n * n for n in range(5)). It makes values one at a time instead of building the whole list, so it saves memory with big data.

questions.text: What does [n * 2 for n in range(3)] produce?
What does [n for n in range(6) if n % 2 == 0] produce?
What is the main advantage of a generator expression?
options: It is always faster than a list
It can be indexed like a list
It can be changed after creation
It produces values one at a time and saves memory

lessons.title: Classes and objects

questions.text: When does __init__ run?
options: Automatically when a new object is created
Only when you call it by name

questions.text: What does self refer to inside a method?
What does 'class Puppy(Dog)' mean?
options: Puppy is a list of Dogs

skills.title: Photoshop Basics
skills.description: Edit and compose images with layers and tools.

lessons.title: Layer masks
lessons.content:
A layer mask hides or shows parts of a layer without deleting any pixels. Select the layer, click the Add Layer Mask button, then paint on the mask with a brush.

On a mask, white shows the layer, black hides it, and shades of gray make it partly transparent. Because nothing is erased, you can paint white again to bring the hidden part back.

questions.text: On a layer mask, what does painting with black do?
options: Shows that part of the layer
Hides that part of the layer

questions.text: Why is a mask better than the Eraser tool?
options: It is non-destructive, so you can restore pixels

lessons.title: Adjustment layers
lessons.content:
Adjustment layers such as Curves, Hue/Saturation and Brightness/Contrast sit above your image and change how it looks without altering the original pixels. You can reopen, change or delete them at any time.

By default an adjustment affects every layer below it. To limit it to the layer directly under it, create a clipping mask by Alt-clicking (Option-clicking on Mac) the line between the two layers.

questions.text: What is the main benefit of an adjustment layer?
options: It can be edited or removed without changing the pixels

questions.text: How do you limit an adjustment layer to one layer?

lessons.title: Smart Objects
lessons.content:
Right-click a layer and choose Convert to Smart Object. Photoshop then keeps the original image data inside the layer. You can shrink it and enlarge it again without losing quality, which is not true for a normal pixel layer.

Filters applied to a Smart Object become Smart Filters. They stay editable and can be turned off or changed later. Double-click the Smart Object to open and edit its contents.

questions.text: What happens when you scale a normal pixel layer down and then back up?
options: It loses detail and looks blurry

questions.text: What is special about a filter applied to a Smart Object?
options: It stays editable as a Smart Filter

questions.text: Which layer type keeps the original image data when resized?

lessons.title: Blend modes
lessons.content:
Blend modes decide how a layer mixes with the layers below. Multiply darkens: white disappears and darker colors remain, which is great for shadows. Screen lightens: black disappears, which is great for glows and light effects.

Overlay increases contrast by combining Multiply and Screen, and Soft Light does the same more gently. Color applies only the hue and saturation of the top layer.

questions.text: In Multiply mode, which color effectively disappears?
In Screen mode, which color effectively disappears?
Which blend mode is commonly used to add contrast to a texture?

lessons.title: Color modes and output
lessons.content:
Use RGB for anything shown on a screen, because screens mix red, green and blue light. Use CMYK for print, because printers mix cyan, magenta, yellow and black ink. Converting RGB to CMYK can dull very bright colors.

For print, work at about 300 pixels per inch at the final size. For export, use JPEG for photos, PNG when you need transparency, PSD to keep layers, and TIFF for high-quality print files.

questions.text: Which color mode is correct for a social media image?
What resolution is typical for a print file at its final size?
Which format keeps a logo's transparent background for the web?

lessons.title: Frequency separation
lessons.content:
Frequency separation splits a portrait into two layers. The low frequency layer holds color and tone. The high frequency layer holds fine texture such as pores and hair.

With this split you can smooth blotchy skin color on the low layer and repair small blemishes on the high layer, while the natural texture stays intact. Over-smoothing the low layer or removing too much from the high layer makes skin look plastic.

questions.text: What does the low frequency layer contain?
Why do retouchers use frequency separation?
options: To fix color and blemishes without destroying skin texture

questions.text: Which layer do you use to smooth blotchy skin color?

skills.title: Flutter Fundamentals
skills.description: Build mobile apps with Flutter and Dart.

lessons.title: Row, Column and Expanded
lessons.content:
Row places its children horizontally and Column places them vertically. Use mainAxisAlignment to space children along the main direction and crossAxisAlignment for the other direction.

Wrap a child in Expanded to make it take the remaining space along the main axis. Two Expanded children share the space equally, or you can give them a flex value to split it in a ratio such as 2 to 1.

questions.text: In which direction does a Column place its children?
What does Expanded do inside a Row?
options: Fills the remaining space along the row

lessons.title: Basic navigation
lessons.content:
Navigator manages a stack of screens. To open a new screen: Navigator.push(context, MaterialPageRoute(builder: (_) => DetailPage())). The new screen sits on top of the stack.

To go back, call Navigator.pop(context). You can also send data back by passing a value to pop and awaiting the result of push.

questions.text: Which call returns to the previous screen?
What does Navigator.push do?
options: Puts a new screen on top of the stack

lessons.title: setState and build
lessons.content:
In a StatefulWidget, the screen only updates when you call setState(() { ... }) after changing a variable. setState marks the widget as needing a rebuild and Flutter then runs build again.

Changing a variable without setState does not refresh the UI. Keep build fast and free of side effects such as network calls, because Flutter may call build many times.

questions.text: What happens if you change a state variable without calling setState?
What does setState do?
Why should you avoid network calls directly inside build?
options: Network calls are not allowed in Dart

lessons.title: Future, async and await

questions.text: Where can the await keyword be used?
What does Future<String> mean?
options: A String that is already available
A String that will be available later
A String that cannot be empty

questions.text: What does FutureBuilder do?
options: Creates a new Future from a widget
Converts a Future to a List
Builds UI based on the state of a Future

lessons.title: State management with ChangeNotifier and Provider
lessons.content:
When several screens need the same data, keep it in one place instead of inside a single widget. A class that extends ChangeNotifier holds the data and calls notifyListeners() after it changes.

Provider makes that object available to the widgets below it. context.watch<T>() listens and rebuilds the widget when data changes. context.read<T>() reads the object once without listening, and is the right choice inside button handlers.

questions.text: What does notifyListeners() do?
options: Tells listening widgets that the data changed

questions.text: Which call should you use inside an onPressed handler?
Why move shared data out of a single widget?
options: So several screens can use the same data

lessons.title: Performance: builders, const and keys
lessons.content:
ListView.builder creates items only when they are about to appear on screen, so long lists stay fast. A plain ListView with thousands of children builds them all at once.

Use const constructors for widgets that never change, so Flutter can reuse them. Use Keys when items in a list can be reordered or removed and each item holds its own state; the key lets Flutter match each state to the right item.

questions.text: What is the benefit of ListView.builder?
options: It builds only the items that are visible or about to be

questions.text: When do Keys matter most?
options: When items in a list reorder or are removed and hold state

questions.text: What is a const widget?
options: A widget that cannot be shown
A widget for constants in math
A widget that can be reused and is not rebuilt unnecessarily

skills.title: Guitar Basics
skills.description: Learn to play guitar from the first chords.

lessons.title: Open chords: Em, Am, D and A
lessons.content:
Four chords unlock hundreds of songs. Em (E minor) needs only two fingers, on the second fret of the A and D strings. Am (A minor) uses three fingers. D and A are bright major chords.

Watch which strings to strum: for D, start on the fourth (D) string and avoid the two lowest strings. For A, start from the fifth (A) string. Let every string ring clearly before you change chords.

questions.text: How many fingers does an Em chord need?
Which string do you start strumming from for the D chord?

lessons.title: Strumming patterns
lessons.content:
Count eighth notes as '1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &'. A popular beginner pattern is down, down-up, up-down-up: strum down on 1, 2 and the 'and' of 2, then up on the 'and' of 3, and so on.

Keep your strumming hand moving in a steady down-up motion even when you do not hit the strings. This keeps the rhythm even. Practice slowly with a metronome and speed up only when it is clean.

questions.text: How do you count eighth notes?
What is a good habit for strumming?
options: Stop the hand when you miss a string
Keep the hand moving in a steady down-up motion

lessons.title: Barre chords
lessons.content:
In a barre chord your index finger presses across all six strings at the same fret, acting like a movable nut. The other fingers then form a shape, such as the E shape, in front of it.

The E-shape barre chord moves up the neck: the barre at the 1st fret is F, at the 3rd fret is G, and at the 5th fret is A. Use the bony side of your index finger, keep your thumb behind the neck, and press evenly. Buzzing usually comes from uneven pressure or finger placement.

questions.text: What does the index finger do in a barre chord?
options: Presses all six strings on the same fret

questions.text: An E-shape barre chord with the barre at the 3rd fret is which chord?
What usually causes buzzing in a barre chord?

lessons.title: The minor pentatonic scale
lessons.content:
The minor pentatonic scale has five notes and is the basis of countless rock and blues solos. In A minor the notes are A, C, D, E and G.

The first pattern, called box 1, sits around the 5th fret. Because the scale leaves out the notes that clash most with typical chords, it is hard to hit a bad note, which makes it ideal for improvising over a backing track.

questions.text: How many notes are in a pentatonic scale?
Which are the notes of the A minor pentatonic scale?
Why is the pentatonic scale good for improvising?
options: It fits many chords and is hard to play wrong
It only works on one string

lessons.title: Fingerstyle and Travis picking
lessons.content:
In fingerstyle you pluck with your fingers instead of a pick. Notation uses p for the thumb, i for the index, m for the middle and a for the ring finger.

In Travis picking the thumb plays a steady alternating bass on the lower strings while the fingers pick the melody on the higher strings. Start slowly with just the thumb pattern until it runs on its own, then add the fingers.

questions.text: In fingerstyle notation, what does 'p' stand for?
What does the thumb do in Travis picking?
options: Plays the melody on high strings

questions.text: What do the fingers usually play in Travis picking?

lessons.title: Using a capo and transposing
lessons.content:
A capo clamps across the neck and shortens the strings, raising the pitch of all strings by one semitone per fret. It lets you play easy open shapes in higher keys.

For example, a G shape with the capo at fret 2 sounds as A, and an E shape with the capo at fret 5 sounds as A. To find the sounding chord, count the capo fret in semitones up from the shape's name.

questions.text: You play an E shape with a capo at fret 5. Which chord sounds?
You play a G shape with a capo at fret 2. Which chord sounds?
What does a capo do?
options: Raises the pitch of all strings equally

skills.title: UI/UX Design Basics
skills.description: Design products that are clear and pleasant to use.

lessons.title: User research: interviews and personas
lessons.content:
User interviews help you learn what people really do and need. Ask open-ended questions such as 'Tell me about the last time you booked a trip' instead of leading questions such as 'Do you like our booking page?'.

A persona is a fictional profile built from the patterns you find in real research. It gives the team a shared picture of who they are designing for, including goals and frustrations.

questions.text: Which is a good interview question?
options: Tell me about the last time you booked a trip.
Don't you think our app is easy?
Would you pay for this feature?

questions.text: What is a persona?
options: A fictional profile built from real research

lessons.title: Usability heuristics
lessons.content:
Jakob Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics are rules of thumb for good interfaces. Examples: visibility of system status (show progress), match between the system and the real world (use familiar words), consistency and standards, and error prevention.

A progress bar during upload follows 'visibility of system status'. A confirmation step before deleting an account follows 'error prevention'.

questions.text: A progress bar during a file upload follows which heuristic?
A confirmation dialog before deleting an account follows which heuristic?

lessons.title: Information architecture and card sorting
lessons.content:
Information architecture (IA) is how content is organized and labeled so people can find it. Card sorting is a research method where participants group topic cards in a way that makes sense to them. In an open card sort they create and name their own groups; in a closed card sort they use groups you provide.

Use the words your users use for labels, not internal jargon. Keep important items within a few clicks of the home screen.

questions.text: What is card sorting used for?
options: Learning how users group and name content

questions.text: In an open card sort, what do participants do?
options: Create and name their own groups

questions.text: Why should labels avoid internal jargon?

lessons.title: Accessibility basics
lessons.content:
Accessible design works for people with different abilities. Text should have enough contrast with its background: WCAG asks for at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text. Do not use color alone to carry meaning, for example add an icon or label to an error besides making it red.

Give images alt text so screen reader users know what they show. Make touch targets large enough, and make sure everything can be reached with a keyboard or screen reader.

questions.text: What is the minimum contrast ratio WCAG asks for normal text?
Why not rely on color alone to show an error?
options: Some users cannot distinguish the colors

questions.text: Who is alt text mainly for?

lessons.title: Usability testing and metrics
lessons.content:
In a usability test, real users try tasks on your design while you observe. In the think-aloud method, participants say what they are thinking as they work. Testing with about five users per round usually reveals most major problems.

Common measures: task success rate (the percentage who complete a task), time on task, and the System Usability Scale (SUS), a standard 10-question survey of perceived usability.

questions.text: What is the think-aloud method?
options: Users say their thoughts while doing tasks

questions.text: What does the System Usability Scale measure?
options: Perceived usability from a standard questionnaire

questions.text: What is task success rate?
options: Percentage of participants who complete the task

lessons.title: Design systems and design tokens
lessons.content:
A design system is a shared set of reusable components, rules and guidelines that keeps a product consistent and speeds up work. Design tokens are named values for design decisions such as colors, spacing and type sizes.

Name tokens by purpose, such as color-danger, rather than by value, such as red. Then a theme change only updates the token's value, and every screen that uses it stays consistent.

questions.text: What is a design token?
options: A named value for a design decision, like a color or spacing

questions.text: What is a main benefit of a design system?
Why name a token 'color-danger' instead of 'red'?
options: The meaning stays the same if the color changes
